editorialPurpose: Understand how simultaneous looking and moving, rapid retinal motion, reduced sensitivity and visual masking differ from watching a recording afterward.
storyAngle: The eyes doing the observing are the eyes making the movement; later playback changes that timing.

segments.text: Look from one eye to the other in a mirror. Why can't you normally catch the movement?
Now record your eyes, and watch it back. There it is.
Each quick jump is a saccade.
In the mirror, the eyes you're watching are also the eyes doing the looking.
As they turn, the image sweeps across the retina.
Visual sensitivity drops around the movement. That's saccadic suppression.
The clear views before and after can also mask the brief blur.
You aren't completely blind. These effects help keep vision stable.
Watching a recording later separates the movement from your own eye turn.
The mirror never stopped showing it. Your visual system normally keeps the sweep out of awareness.

narrativeStructure.purpose: Camera icon beside same mirror portrait, then visibly transition to later playback with a moving iris. Recorded external view, not direct mirror perception.

narrativeStructure.purpose: Carry eye and retinal sweep into a softly attenuated feature illustration; qualitative dip spans before/during/after, never a flat zero or blackout.

narrativeStructure.purpose: Same eye closeup expands into before/blur/after sequence, then clear flank views visually dominate. Label perception schematic, time expanded.

narrativeStructure.purpose: First-person mirror view shifts gaze target and resolves without black frames; stable perception illustration, not literal subjective recording or complete explanation of spatial constancy.

narrativeStructure.purpose: Return to original person/mirror with continuous reflected movement on external view; momentary direct-perception annotation and confident resolved ending.
